title: On-call and Incident Response Playbook (Comprehensive)
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This document is Redwood Inference's canonical on-call and incident response playbook. It covers the incident lifecycle (detection, triage, mitigation, recovery), runbooks for common failure modes, postmortem requirements, on-call rotation and escalation policies, game day planning, and templates for status page and customer communications. The playbook is intended for engineers, SREs, and support staff who participate in incident response.

Scope and goals
- Scope: incidents affecting customer-facing inference (API), model-serving control plane, routing, and underlying GPU capacity.
- Goals: restore service safely, minimize customer impact, preserve data integrity, and learn via timely postmortems.
- Primary SLAs/SLOs (reference):
  - API availability: 99.95% monthly
  - p95 request latency (inference): < 200 ms for small models; model-specific p95 in model catalog
  - Error budget: 0.05% monthly

Incident severity classification
1) Sev 1 (Critical)
   - Customer-facing outage or severe degradation impacting > 10% of production traffic or major account(s).
   - Immediate conference bridge, paging on-call, exec notification.
2) Sev 2 (High)
   - Significant partial degradation (reduced throughput, increased p95 latency) impacting 1-10% of traffic or a single large customer.
   - Page on-call and follow escalation.
3) Sev 3 (Medium)
   - Minor degradation, non-urgent performance regressions, or isolated errors.
   - Triage asynchronously; may be handled in-duty hours.
4) Sev 4 (Low)
   - Informational, maintenance, or scheduled work with no customer impact.

Incident lifecycle (high-level procedure)
1) Detect
   - Alerts via PagerDuty/SMS/Slack, automated monitoring (metrics, logs, traces), customer reports.
   - On-call engineer acknowledges within 5 minutes for Sev 1/2.
2) Triage
   - Determine scope: services, customers, regions, model variants.
   - Collect evidence: error rates, warm/cold cache signals, GPU metrics (util, memory), control plane logs.
   - Assign severity and incident commander (IC).
3) Mitigate
   - Apply first-line mitigations (traffic routing, autoscale, fallback model variant, increase replicas, restart pods).
   - Use runbooks for known failure modes (see Runbooks section).
4) Communicate
   - Internal: update #incidents Slack channel every 15-30 minutes for Sev 1/2. Use the Incident Status template.
   - External: post to status.redwood-inference.com and notify impacted customers per Customer Comms templates.
5) Recover
   - Validate service health with metrics and synthetic checks. Gradually restore traffic and monitor for regressions.
6) Close and Postmortem
   - If Sev 2+ produce a postmortem within 72 hours (draft) and a final postmortem within 7 days. Action items must have owners and due dates.

Roles and responsibilities
- Incident Commander (IC): coordinates response, owns timeline and communications.
- Primary on-call: first responder, executes runbook steps, escalates to IC if needed.
- Secondary on-call / Escalation: provides backup and deeper system knowledge.
- Owner teams: service owners responsible for root cause and follow-up fixes.
- Communications lead: drafts external status updates and customer messages.

Escalation matrix (summary)
- On-call engineer -> Team lead (15 min unresolved for Sev 1) -> Eng SRE lead -> CTO/VP Eng (if > 60 min unresolved and major customer impact).

Runbooks (common incidents)
Note: each runbook below lists quick checks, commands, and mitigation steps. Always coordinate with IC before broad changes.

Runbook A: Control plane unresponsive\- Symptoms: API returns 503 for routing calls; control-plane healthcheck failing.
- Quick checks:
  1. Check control-plane pods: kubectl get pods -n control-plane
  2. Inspect logs: kubectl logs -n control-plane <pod> --since=15m
  3. Check database connectivity: psql -c "SELECT 1" on control-plane DB replica
- Mitigations:
  1. If pods unhealthy, try rolling restart: kubectl rollout restart deployment/control-plane
  2. If DB connection errors, fail traffic to Dedicated pools and enable degraded mode (see routing fallback).
  3. If persistent, scale up replicas temporarily: kubectl scale deployment/control-plane --replicas=<N+2>
- Escalation: Eng infra and DB owner.

Runbook B: Model-serving latency spike (p95 elevated)\- Symptoms: p95 latency increases beyond SLO, increased GPU utilization or cache miss rate.
- Quick checks:
  1. Confirm metric anomalies: Grafana dashboard "inference-latency" and "kv-cache-hit-rate"
  2. Check model variant routing and recent rollouts in Redwood Console.
  3. Inspect GPU metrics: nvidia-smi (on host), cloud provider instance metrics.
- Mitigations:
  1. If new rollout suspected, rollback to previous stable model variant. Use Redwood Console -> Rollouts -> Abort/rollback.
  2. Enable model fallback to quantized/cheaper variant for latency-critical routes.
  3. Warm caches: run synthetic traffic against hot prefixes or pre-warm KV cache.
  4. Temporarily increase concurrency limits or add serving replicas.
- Escalation: Runtime team and model-onboarding owners.

Runbook C: GPU OOM or node-level failures\- Symptoms: OOM kube events, pods crashlooping on worker nodes.
- Quick checks:
  1. kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -i oom
  2. Check node allocatable memory and pod requests: kubectl describe node <node>
  3. Review recent autoscaler or job failures.
- Mitigations:
  1. Evacuate affected node (cordon/drain) and restart pods on healthy nodes: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
  2. If persistent, reduce per-pod GPU memory request or switch to multi-GPU packing profile.
  3. Clear large cache entries or limit max sequence length for impacted routes.
- Escalation: GPU fleet owner and infra on-call.

Runbook D: KV cache thrashing / cold cache\- Symptoms: cache hit-rate drops, upstream latency increases but no CPU/GPU saturation.
- Quick checks:
  1. Inspect cache metrics: cache_hit_rate, cache_evictions.
  2. Confirm traffic pattern change or new prompt set.
- Mitigations:
  1. Increase cache capacity policy for hot tenants or classes of requests.
  2. Temporarily route critical customers to pre-warmed pools.
  3. If caused by a bad rollout, rollback rollout.
- Escalation: Runtime team and routing engineers.

Runbook templates and safety checks\- Before any database/schema migration or large rollout, follow the change management checklist (see policies-and-process/change-management).
- Safety: avoid destructive actions without coordination. For high-impact mitigations (DB failover, large-scale restart), get approver from Eng SRE.

On-call rotations and handoffs
- Rotation cadence: teams typically use 1-week rotations for primary on-call and 1-week for secondary (overlapping). Critical services may adopt 4-day rotations for faster recovery.
- Handoff checklist (must be completed at end of shift):
  1. Update duty status in the on-call roster.
  2. Review open incidents and summarize next steps in Slack #incidents.
  3. Confirm runbook steps taken and outstanding action items.
  4. Mention any scheduled maintenance or game days.
- On-call tooling: PagerDuty for paging, Slack #incidents for internal comms, Redwood Console for rollouts and model metrics, Grafana dashboards, and status.redwood-inference.com for external.

Game days and preparedness exercises
- Purpose: validate runbooks, surface gaps in instrumentation, test communication channels and handoffs.
- Frequency: at least quarterly per team owning critical services; cross-team full-stack game days twice per year.
- Example 1-day game day schedule:
  - 09:00 - Kickoff and objectives (IC and observers)
  - 09:15 - Simulated incident injected (e.g., model-serving latency spike)
  - 09:15-10:30 - Response window: execute runbooks, document timeline
  - 10:30-11:00 - Debrief and identify telemetry gaps
  - 11:00-12:00 - Design quick mitigations and assign follow-ups
  - 13:00-15:00 - Implement instrumentation improvements or runbook updates
  - 15:00-16:00 - Final review and publish game day notes
- Game day success metrics: time-to-detect, time-to-acknowledge, time-to-restore.

Postmortem requirements and template
- For Sev 2+ incidents: initial draft within 72 hours; final postmortem within 7 days. Postmortem must be published in confluence under confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems and linked to the incident record.
- Postmortem template (required sections):
  1. Title (short descriptive)
  2. Summary (one-paragraph impact and outcome)
  3. Detection timeline (list of timestamps and actions)
  4. Root cause analysis (technical RCA)
  5. Contributing factors (process, SLO assumptions, flaky telemetry)
  6. Customer impact (number of affected requests/customers, downtime window)
  7. Mitigations applied (temporary and long-term)
  8. Action items (owner and due date)
  9. Lessons learned and follow-ups
  10. Related artifacts (logs, dashboards, PRs, runbook versions)

Postmortem scoring and follow-through
- Action items must be tracked in the team backlog; owners should update status weekly until complete.
- A postmortem review meeting (15-30 minutes) should be scheduled within 14 days for Sev 1 incidents.

Status page and customer communications templates
- Use status.redwood-inference.com for public updates. Communications lead approves all public messages for Sev 1/Sev 2. Internal incident updates go to #incidents channel.

Template: Initial acknowledgment (public)
- Title: "Incident: [short description] - Investigating"
- Body: "We are aware of an issue affecting [service/region/customers]. Our on-call team is investigating. Impact: [e.g., 503s on API endpoints, higher latency]. Time detected: [UTC timestamp]. We will provide updates every [15/30] minutes. Status page: [link]."

Template: Customer-facing update (example)
- Subject: "Update: [short description] - Partial mitigation in place"
- Body: "We have implemented [mitigation] which has reduced impact by [estimate]. A subset of customers may still see degraded performance. We will continue to monitor and update at [time]. If you are experiencing issues, please contact support@redwood-inference.com and include request IDs if available."

Template: Resolution message (public)
- Title: "Resolved: [short description]"
- Body: "The incident affecting [service] has been resolved as of [UTC timestamp]. Root cause: [brief RCA]. Actions taken: [list]. Next steps: [postmortem link and action items]. We apologize for the impact to customers. For support, contact support@redwood-inference.com."

Internal incident update cadence (Sev 1/2)
- Every 15 minutes: short summary including time, impact, actions taken, next steps, owner.
- Once mitigation stabilizes: every 30 minutes until resolved.

Recording incidents and metrics
- Record all incidents in the incident tracker (Jira/Confluence incident index). Include links to traces, logs, and Grafana panels.
- Metrics to capture per incident: detect_time, ack_time, restore_time, total_downtime, affected_requests_count, estimated_customers_impacted.

Training and on-call health
- New hires must shadow an on-call rotation for one sprint and complete the on-call orientation checklist.
- Limit consecutive on-call weeks to no more than 3 without an offset week.
- Encourage post-incident rotations if a team experiences > 2 Sev 2+ incidents in a month to prevent burnout.

Appendices
A) Quick command cheat-sheet
- kubectl get pods -n <ns>
- kubectl logs -f <pod> -n <ns> --since=10m\- kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> -n <ns>
- systemctl status redis (for onprem replicas)
- nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY

B) Contact & escalation directory (abbreviated)
- Eng SRE on-call: pager duty (primary) and Slack #eng-sre-oncall
- Runtime lead: Marcus Patel (pager)
- Infra lead: Riley Torres (pager)
- Customer comms: Samantha Green (email: customer-comms@redwood-inference.com)

C) Change management pre-deploy checklist (summary)
- Confirm health of canary metrics
- Confirm rollback plan exists and tested
- Notify on-call and schedule maintenance window if required

Document maintenance
- Owner: Engineering (Eng SRE). Review cadence: every 6 months or after each Sev 1 incident.
- Update this page with new runbooks, escalation changes, or tooling updates.
